families.s: HSE rubber-manufacturing, tyre and rubber-dust guidance
families.t: rubber chemistry, dust and fume, machinery, tyre handling, fire, storage, COSHH, ventilation and industry plans
f: Rubber manufacture combines heavy processing machinery with continually developing rubber chemistry.
Health controls should address rubber dust, fume and process chemicals.
Rubber dust and fume exposure requires COSHH assessment and effective source and ventilation controls.
Industry guidance covers general rubber goods, new tyres, retreading, distribution and tyre recovery.
Shredded rubber and tyre crumb can self-heat and require fire-aware storage controls.
Machinery, manual handling, workplace transport, slips and stress are relevant industry risks.
Tyre collection, delivery, storage and handling need controls for load security and vehicle interfaces.
Employers should monitor control performance and use industry guidance and action plans to reduce accidents and ill health.
families.g: Rubber-industry risk depends on formulation, temperature, dust and fume generation, machinery, tyre size and storage, fire load, ventilation, maintenance and work organisation.

families.s: HSE ceramics-industry injury and occupational-health guidance
families.t: handling, slips, moving machinery, silica, kilns, dermatitis, ergonomics, extraction and COSHH controls
f: Important ceramics injuries arise from handling, slips and trips, moving or falling objects and moving machinery.
Musculoskeletal disorders and dermatitis are significant occupational-health concerns in ceramics.
Non-metallic-mineral work commonly requires control of dust, moving machinery, manual handling and falls.
Ceramic raw materials and finishing processes can generate respirable crystalline silica.
RCS exposure can cause silicosis and other serious lung disease and should be prevented or adequately controlled.
Kilns require suitable siting, temperature controls, maintenance, ventilation and protection from hot surfaces.
Handling and repetitive tasks should be redesigned or assisted to reduce musculoskeletal risk.
Enclosure, extraction, wet methods, housekeeping and suitable RPE may be needed for residual dust risk.
families.g: Ceramics risk depends on silica content, process, kiln and machinery, dustiness, handling, extraction, cleaning, heat, chemicals and worker exposure duration.

families.s: HSE molten-metal explosion, lifting and protective-clothing guidance
families.t: water contamination, scrap preparation, furnaces, lifting, exclusion, PPE, supervision and emergency control
f: Water contamination of molten metal can cause violent explosions.
Scrap should be stored dry where possible and checked and prepared before charging a furnace.
Containers and drums in scrap require controls to prevent retained liquid entering molten metal.
Workers need information, training and supervision on contamination, charging and safe furnace practice.
Overhead-crane and other lifting operations must be properly planned, supervised and carried out by competent people.
Suitable molten-metal protective clothing is required where other controls cannot remove splash risk.
PPE selection follows assessment of the metal, quantity, temperature, splash pattern and work position.
Buildings, floors, routes, moulds, dies and weather protection should prevent water ingress, ejection and trips.
families.g: Molten-metal safety depends on metal and temperature, water exclusion, charge preparation, furnace and mould condition, lifting, routes, splash exposure, PPE and emergency response.

families.s: HSE foundry dust, fume, mist and vibration health guidance
families.t: RCS, foundry fume, asthma, lung cancer, spray mist, COSHH, LEV, RPE, surveillance and vibration
f: Foundry sand, fettling and kiln-lining dust can contain respirable crystalline silica.
Inhaling RCS can cause silicosis, a serious and irreversible lung disease.
Molten-metal fume is hazardous and ferrous foundry fume can cause lung cancer.
Other foundry fumes and spray mists can cause asthma and other lung disease.
COSHH requires foundry dust, fume and mist exposure to be prevented or adequately controlled.
Controls should combine effective extraction, suitable RPE, supervision, maintenance and exposure records.
Health surveillance and monitoring should identify early disease and demonstrate that controls remain effective.
Hand-held powered tools used in fettling and finishing can create hand-arm vibration risk requiring control.
families.g: Foundry health risk depends on metal and binder chemistry, sand silica content, process temperature, dust and mist generation, extraction, RPE, maintenance, duration and surveillance.
